query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Partially reducing the Mo content by substituting a portion of Mo with Nb in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will lower the overall electronegativity difference and alleviate excessive local lattice distortions, thereby enhancing room-temperature ductility while maintaining most of the high yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, disordered BCC NbZrTiHfMo with a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa but limited plasticity due to high Mo-induced electronegativity differences.
generation.intervention: Replace a fraction of Mo with Nb (for example, targeting a Mo:Nb ratio that shifts from 1:1 to a composition such as Nb0.5Mo0.5 in the Mo site) so that the overall composition remains near-equiatomic but with reduced Mo content.
generation.conditions: Process under similar casting and homogenization conditions at room temperature; mechanical properties should be measured in standard compressive tests. The substitution level must be optimized (e.g., 25–50% Mo replaced) so that the BCC solid solution is retained.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in the local electronegativity mismatch and lattice distortion; modification of the dislocation-solute interaction environment leading to a less brittle dislocation core.
generation.mechanism: Mo is known to enhance strength via solid solution strengthening but also increases the electronegativity difference, which promotes brittleness by hindering dislocation mobility. Nb, having a lower electronegativity compared to Mo, can provide similar solid solution strengthening while reducing the charge-transfer fluctuations and local stress fields. This adjustment is anticipated to ease dislocation glide (possibly promoting both edge and screw motion) and thus improve ductility without a large sacrifice of strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to retain a compressive yield strength close to 1700 MPa while exhibiting significantly greater plastic strain (an improvement in ductility compared to the original limited-plasticity state).
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy with a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa and reduced room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated if the Mo substitution does not exceed a threshold (likely below full replacement) beyond which the solid solution strengthening diminishes; excessive reduction of Mo or over-substitution may lead to an unwanted drop in strength or phase instability.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines the elemental subtraction insights from the study in PMC7514121 (which demonstrated that Mo enhances strength but compromises ductility in high-entropy alloys) with the concept that reducing the average electronegativity difference (as discussed in PMC6504951) can improve dislocation mobility. What is new is the proposal to use a targeted, partial Mo-to-Nb substitution in NbZrTiHfMo specifically to balance strength and plasticity at room temperature. The precise substitution fraction and its effects on dislocation behavior remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys where Mo is partially replaced by Nb in varying fractions (e.g., 0%, 25%, 50%, and 75% substitution of the Mo component) while keeping the other elements (Nb, Zr, Ti, Hf) constant. Process each alloy under identical conditions to obtain a disordered BCC structure. Perform room-temperature compressive testing and microstructural analysis (e.g., via TEM and XRD) to assess phase stability and dislocation characteristics.
measurements: Microstructural evaluation of phase homogeneity and dislocation behavior
Determination of lattice parameters and electronegativity-related distortions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if partial substitution of Mo with Nb does not increase the compressive plasticity while maintaining a yield strength near 1700 MPa, or if the modified alloys undergo phase transitions or exhibit unstable dislocation structures, compared to the baseline equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.

AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.
